description_full: McDonald's Corporation owns, operates, and franchises restaurants under the McDonald's brand in the United States and internationally. It offers food and beverages, including hamburgers and cheeseburgers, various chicken sandwiches, fries, shakes, frozen desserts, sundaes, soft serve cones, cookies, pies, soft drinks, coffee, and other beverages; and full or limited breakfast, as well as sells various other products during limited-time promotions. The company owns and operates franchised restaurants under various structures, including conventional franchise, developmental license, or affiliate. McDonald's Corporation was founded in 1940 and is based in Chicago, Illinois.
ceo_bio: Mr. Christopher J. Kempczinski | Chairman President, & CEO | Age 56 | Compensation: $4.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 150K people. Revenue per employee of $179K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers. Each employee generates $48K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $1K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 26× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10). Recent headlines include layoff or workforce-reduction announcements.
financial_summary: McDonald's Corporation is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $192.0B market cap on $26.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 29% against a 7% cost of capital — a 22-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $7.2B in free cash flow — roughly 27 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.23× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 7.8×.

Shareholder yield of 3.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 5.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Piotroski score 3/9 — the fundamentals are deteriorating on multiple fronts
Carries a 53% premium to sector median EV/EBITDA (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Financial quality metrics lag Consumer Cyclical peers
Recent layoff news — often the market’s first signal that growth is under pressure or costs are being rebased
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 39% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
50 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

sect: Its 46% operating margin runs 39pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 5.81x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 2.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 21% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 20% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 21% and a beta of 0.49, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.3B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2020 crash, 17% in the 2022 bear market and 21% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $244 (margin of safety -11%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 4%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $169 to $357 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 16.4 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 26.7 vs 16.7 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-6%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 29 covering analysts target $299 on average, 10% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 29% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 22pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.16).
It converts 27% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.23x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.2x net debt to EBITDA ($774.0M of cash against $41.5B of debt), with interest covered 7.8x.
The current ratio of 0.95 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.1% over 3 years, 7.0% over 5 years and 0.6% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 20% of profits supports about 5.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.2% a year over five years.
Capex runs 7.4x depreciation (12.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 76%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (8 sales, net $3.8M sold).
It returns 3.7% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 2.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 50 consecutive years, raising it 6.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 150,000 employees, each generates about $179K of revenue, 0.5x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $48K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.6M (26x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
